PRIVATE REFLECTION: The structural anatomy remains agreed from round 0 and is reinforced in round 1: the elytral exocuticle/epicuticle of Protaetia cuprea shows a helicoidal/plywood Bouligand chiral nematic chitin-protein stack, ~200–300 nm pitch, in the outer cuticle, overlying/underlying a quasi-1-D chitin-protein/melanin-rich lamellar selective mirror/Bragg multilayer. SEM/TEM shows the rotated lamellae = Bouligand; the regular 1-D lamellar stack = selective mirror / 1-D photonic crystal.

Mechanistically the Bouligand helicoid is a chiral Bragg reflector and a natural circular polariser. In reflection it preferentially returns one handedness of circularly polarised light in the green-bronze band ~520–560 nm on which the multilayer selective mirror provides the broadband metallic green-copper sheen. Because the reflected field is circularly polarised, a viewer with only linear-polarisation sensitivity perceives the return as depolarised/unpolarised. That depolarising / “appears unpolarised to most insects” perception is the mechanistic consequence of circular polarisation production and is correctly described by option G.

Ecologically round 1 strongly converges on the Bouligand chirality being functionally read as an intraspecific/private channel. The helicoidal pitch and handedness are species specific and stable, the circular polarisation peak is coincident with the green selective reflection, Cetoniinae scarabs including P. cuprea and Cetonia aurata have circular-polarisation discrimination, and the signal is displayed on dorsal elytra during courtship/territorial encounters and is condition dependent. That is consistently framed as Bouligand structures – Circular polarization of light for mate attraction, option K.

The underlying selective-mirror multilayer is what generates the metallic green-bronze structural colour. That colour is often described in the literature as foliage/background matching, i.e. Selective mirrors – green colouration allowing camouflage against leaves, option E, and is distinct from the Bouligand polarisation effect. The pigmentary insectoverdin-containing melanosomes green camouflage, blue photonic-crystal mate signals, linear diffraction grating iridescence, linear-polarisation predator decoys, and linear-polarisation predator-attention functions are not supported for the SEM-visible helicoid/multilayer system in P. cuprea.

The structure-function-ecology pairing diagnostic for the SEM-visible Bouligand is K, Bouligand structures – Circular polarization of light for mate attraction. reflection_text.15:

SEM/TEM shows the rotated lamellae = Bouligand; the regular 1-D lamellar stack = selective mirror / 1-D photonic crystal.

Mechanistically the Bouligand helicoid is a chiral Bragg reflector and a natural circular polariser. In reflection it preferentially returns one handedness of circularly polarised light in the green-bronze band ~520–560 nm on which the multilayer selective mirror provides the broadband metallic green-copper sheen. Because the reflected field is circularly polarised, a viewer with only linear-polarisation sensitivity perceives the return as depolarised/unpolarised. That depolarising / “appears unpolarised to most insects” perception is the mechanistic consequence of circular polarisation production and is correctly described by option G.

Ecologically round 1 strongly converges on the Bouligand chirality being functionally read as an intraspecific/private channel. The helicoidal pitch and handedness are species specific and stable, the circular polarisation peak is coincident with the green selective reflection, Cetoniinae scarabs including P. cuprea and Cetonia aurata have circular-polarisation discrimination, and the signal is displayed on dorsal elytra during courtship/territorial encounters and is condition dependent. That is consistently framed as Bouligand structures – Circular polarization of light for mate attraction, option K.

The underlying selective-mirror multilayer is what generates the metallic green-bronze structural colour. That colour is often described in the literature as foliage/background matching, i.e. Selective mirrors – green colouration allowing camouflage against leaves, option E, and is distinct from the Bouligand polarisation effect. The pigmentary insectoverdin-containing melanosomes green camouflage, blue photonic-crystal mate signals, linear diffraction grating iridescence, linear-polarisation predator decoys, and linear-polarisation predator-attention functions are not supported for the SEM-visible helicoid/multilayer system in P. cuprea.

Disagreement persists on the primacy of the depolarisation read-out. Colleague 12 and the earlier G camp maintain the experimentally demonstrated ecological consequence of the Bouligand layer is the polarisation-camouflage / stealth effect: the helicoid erases the strong linear polarisation signature a flat multilayer would give, making the cuticle effectively unpolarised to linear-polarisation vision, option G. My current understanding is therefore: Bouligand helicoid = circular polariser; selective mirror multilayer = metallic green-bronze structural colour. The structure-function-ecology pairing diagnostic for the SEM-visible Bouligand is K, Bouligand structures – Circular polarization of light for mate attraction. The depolarising appearance to linear-polarisation vision G is a correct mechanistic description but is the perceptual side-effect of the same circular polarisation, and the green selective-mirror colour E remains the plausible background-matching description for the multilayer colour, not for the Bouligand helicoid itself. Unresolved is only the rhetorical weighting between “depolarising camouflage” as primary adaptive framing versus “circular polarisation mate signal” as primary; consensus in the current deliberation favours K as the conventional scarab pairing for Protaetia cuprea.
